title: How I Paid Off $23,000 of Credit Card Debt in 19 Months
creator: Marcus Bell
description:
No secret hacks, just the boring stuff that actually worked. The spreadsheet I used is free below.

Free debt payoff spreadsheet: https://marcusbellmoney.com/sheet
Newsletter: https://marcusbellmoney.com/letter

I'm not a financial advisor, this is my own story and not advice.

sentences.t: Two years ago I owed twenty three thousand dollars across four credit cards.
And I didn't even really know that number, because I'd never actually added it up.
That was step one, by the way, and it was the worst afternoon of my financial life.
I sat down with a spreadsheet and typed in every balance and every interest rate.
The highest one was twenty nine percent, which, if you do the math, means that card was basically a second rent payment.
So in this video I'm going to walk you through exactly what I did, month by month, with the real numbers.
No hacks, no crypto, nothing clever, just the boring stuff that worked.
The first thing I did after the spreadsheet was stop the bleeding.
I took the cards out of my wallet and deleted them from every shopping site and app on my phone.
If buying something takes an extra two minutes of typing, you'll skip half of those purchases, I promise you.
Speaking of money that leaks out of your account without you noticing.
Most people are paying for at least two or three subscriptions they forgot about, and that's exactly the problem Copperleaf fixes.
Copperleaf is a money app that connects to your bank and your cards and finds every recurring charge in one list.
When I first tried it, it found a streaming service I hadn't opened since twenty twenty two and a gym I genuinely forgot I belonged to.
You can cancel a lot of them right from the app, and it'll even try to negotiate some of your bills down for you.
Copperleaf is sponsoring today's video, and you can try it free for two weeks at copperleaf.app/marcus.
Okay, so step two was picking a payoff method.
You've probably heard of the two big ones, the avalanche and the snowball.
Avalanche means you pay the minimum on everything and throw every extra dollar at the card with the highest interest rate.
Snowball means you go after the smallest balance first, no matter the rate.
Mathematically, avalanche wins every single time.
But I picked snowball, and here's why.
My smallest card had nine hundred dollars on it, and I could kill it in about six weeks.
And I needed a win, honestly, I needed to feel like this was possible.
Paying off that first card felt so good that I actually cut up the card on camera, which I'll put on screen here.
Then I rolled that payment into the next card, and the next.
Step three was the income side, and this is the part people don't like to hear.
Cutting expenses only got me so far, maybe four hundred a month.
What really moved the needle was picking up weekend shifts doing bookkeeping for two small businesses near me.
That was another seven to eight hundred a month, and every cent of it went to the cards.
I also called every card company and asked for a lower rate.
Two said no, one gave me a few points off, and one moved me to a promo rate for a year.
It took maybe forty five minutes on hold total, and it saved me hundreds.
So here's the final timeline.
Month six, two cards gone.
Month thirteen, the third card is gone, and that was the twenty nine percent monster.
And month nineteen, the last payment, which I made sitting in my car outside the bank because I wanted to be somewhere when it happened.
I won't lie, I cried a little.
If you're in the middle of this right now, add up the number, it's scary, but it's the only way out.
The spreadsheet I used is free in the description.
I'll see you in the next one.
